items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: The dollar got bought in the selloff and in the recovery. MUFG says that can't last
items.idea: After November's swings the dollar sits at its highest against the majors since the April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, having gained during the AI liquidation and then held up when equities bounced. The weekly giveback was uneven: CAD and AUD +0.71%, NOK +0.55%, CHF +0.44%, EUR only +0.06%, JPY -0.57%. MUFG reads the dispersion as the market trading several stories at once (rates, carry unwind, country risk) instead of one dollar view.
items.angle: A dollar that wins in both risk-off and risk-on is a crowded consensus, not a regime. The dispersion says pick pairs, not DXY.
items.tweetA: The dollar rallied when AI stocks sold off, then held when they bounced. An asset that wins in both states is usually just a crowded one. I'd rather own the pair where the story is cleanest than argue about $DXY.
items.tweetB: Weekly FX scorecard: CAD +0.71%, AUD +0.71%, EUR +0.06%, JPY -0.57%. That's not a dollar move, that's four different trades wearing the same ticker. Single-direction USD views are the wrong tool right now.

charts.desc: Weekly G10 performance bar chart vs USD: CAD/AUD lead, yen the only loser. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: EUR/USD broke 1.10 for the first time since the tariff shock. MUFG's map: 1.05-1.10, then up in 2027
items.idea: EUR/USD hit 1.0881 on Nov 23 and is down 6.6% in 2026 after rising about 13.4% last year (1.0350 to 1.1750). MUFG's analog is 2022, when an energy shock took the pair below parity, but it does not expect a full repeat: the IEA now sees possible excess oil supply next year. Base case is stabilisation in 1.0500-1.1000 and a recovery later in 2027; in 2023 the euro regained about 3.1% once energy pressure faded.
items.angle: The euro call is really an oil call. If you already have a crude view for 2027, you have a EUR/USD view.
items.tweetA: MUFG's 2027 euro recovery needs exactly one thing: energy to stop getting worse. Not growth, not reform. If you're bearish crude into next year, long EUR is the same trade with a crowded short as a kicker.
items.tweetB: EUR/USD: +13.4% last year, -6.6% this year, back under 1.10. Two years of noise and the pair is roughly where the tariff shock left it. The 2022 analog everyone is using ended below parity. The 2023 sequel was +3.1%.

charts.desc: EUR/USD against euro-area energy terms of trade, showing the 2022 collapse and partial 2023 recovery.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: Both the ECB and the Fed are hiking, and MUFG says the ECB matters more for the next euro turn
items.idea: MUFG expects two more ECB hikes by early 2027 to about 3.00%, with headline inflation running at more than twice target. The Fed is expected to hike at least twice more (December and early 2027), fully reversing its 2025 easing. Pressure on both to keep hiking should fade as energy inflation slows from Q2 2027, and by H2 the market could start pricing cuts for late 2027.
items.angle: If both central banks hike in step, the rate differential stops moving and the euro stops falling. The trade is the gap, not the level.
items.tweetA: The Fed is about to un-do every cut from 2025. The ECB is hiking alongside it. When both sides tighten at the same pace, the differential goes nowhere and all that's left is positioning. Positioning is max short euro.
items.tweetB: Timeline worth writing down: hikes through early 2027, energy inflation rolls over from Q2, cuts priced for late 2027. That's a nine-month window where duration goes from untouchable to consensus. I'd rather be early than argue with it.

charts.desc: Policy-rate expectations for ECB and Fed. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: French-German 10-year spread has doubled since mid-year, widest since 2011
items.idea: The OAT-Bund spread has roughly doubled since the middle of the year to its widest since the 2011 sovereign crisis. 2027 is a heavy calendar: an early Spanish election at the end of November, the French presidential vote on April 18 and May 2, and an Italian general election expected in October. A proposed French constitutional 'golden rule' on balanced budgets needs three-fifths of both chambers. Le Pen backs the principle; Sarkozy tried the same in 2011 and failed.
items.angle: MUFG's point is that the premium is already paid, so bad news has a higher bar. The opposing view is that 2011 spreads did not stop at 'widest since'.
items.tweetA: French spreads are at 2011 levels and the response is a constitutional amendment that needs a three-fifths majority in a parliament that can't pass a budget. That's not a fix, that's a press release. The spread is the only honest vote.
items.tweetB: Three of the eurozone's four biggest economies vote within 11 months: Spain, France, Italy. The euro is already -6.6% and OAT-Bund has doubled. Question nobody asks: what does the ECB do if it's hiking into a French election?

charts.desc: 10-year France-Germany spread, back to 2011 crisis levels.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: Leveraged funds are short 76,600 euro contracts, a z-score of -2.13
items.idea: CFTC data show leveraged funds net short about 76,600 euro futures, close to the most bearish positioning since the initial COVID shock in early 2020. MUFG's two-year z-score is about -2.13. The bank says this is not a buy signal alone, but if energy eases, French risk stabilises and the Fed nears its last hike, covering could make the rebound larger than the fundamentals justify.
items.angle: Extreme short plus a catalyst calendar (Dec 1 euro CPI, Dec 4 payrolls) is a setup for a squeeze on any dovish surprise.
items.tweetA: Euro short is at a -2.1 z-score, the most crowded since March 2020. You don't need good news from Europe to get hurt here. You need one soft US payrolls print on Dec 4.
items.tweetB: Everyone is short the euro for three reasons: Fed, France, energy. All three are known, priced and positioned. The best FX recoveries start when bad news stops getting worse, and that's a much lower bar than good news.

charts.desc: Leveraged-fund net euro futures positioning, near the March 2020 extreme.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: One week of IMM flows shows funds cutting every risk currency at once
items.idea: In the week to Nov 17 leveraged funds cut long AUD by 12,839 contracts, long GBP by 5,705 and long MXN by 5,774, while adding 4,911 to euro shorts and 6,935 to yen shorts. Dollar longs are concentrated against CAD and EUR; the largest remaining short-dollar position is against the peso. On z-scores, long BRL and short EUR and CHF are the most stretched.
items.angle: The peso and real are the last carry longs standing. If the liquidation has another leg, that is where the forced selling comes from.
items.tweetA: The most crowded long in FX right now is the Brazilian real. The biggest short-dollar position is still the Mexican peso. In a month when everything else got de-risked, LatAm carry is the trade that hasn't been stopped out yet.
items.tweetB: Funds are short CHF at a stretched z-score during an equity liquidation. Short the safe haven, in a selloff, for carry. I know which side of that I'd rather be on. $FXF

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: Japanese investors sold foreign bonds in 8 of the last 9 weeks while foreigners bought ¥3.55tn of JGBs
items.idea: MoF data show Japanese investors sold about ¥441bn of foreign bonds in the week to Nov 20, net sellers in eight of the prior nine weeks, while buying about ¥1.07tn of overseas equities over four weeks. Foreigners bought roughly ¥3.55tn of Japanese bonds and ¥1.99tn of equities over four weeks. Leveraged funds are still wary of shorting yen after joint US-Japan intervention, but Japanese retail margin traders are rebuilding long USD/JPY and EUR/JPY.
items.angle: The marginal buyer of Treasuries from Japan is absent while the Fed is hiking. That matters more for US term premium than for the yen.
items.tweetA: Japan has been a net seller of foreign bonds in 8 of 9 weeks. Foreigners put ¥3.5 trillion into JGBs in a month. The flow that funded Treasuries for two decades is running in reverse in a year when the 10-year peaked at 5.34%. Not a coincidence.
items.tweetB: Hedge funds won't short the yen because they remember the joint intervention. Japanese retail is doing it anyway. When the pros step back and Mrs. Watanabe steps in, I know who usually provides the exit liquidity.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: MUFG's live trade: short USD/CHF from 0.8400, target 0.8200, stop 0.8550
items.idea: USD/CHF gained almost 4% from its early-November low before reversing; MUFG stays short from 0.8400 (marked around 0.8350), targeting 0.8200 with a stop at 0.8550. The logic is that the franc benefits if AI uncertainty persists and also if tighter US financial conditions pull 2027 Fed pricing lower. It does not need a risk-on recovery, unlike the cyclical currencies.
items.angle: A trade that works in both continued liquidation and a Fed repricing is a hedge with positive seasonality. 150 pips of risk for 200 of reward is thin, though.
items.tweetA: Short USD/CHF is the one dollar-bear trade that doesn't need equities to recover. If AI keeps unwinding, the franc is the haven. If the Fed blinks, the yield gap closes. Add 81% December seasonality and it's the cleanest expression I've seen this week.
items.tweetB: MUFG's stop is 150 pips away and the target is 200. That's a 1.3:1 payoff on a 'high conviction' call. The idea is good. The structure tells you how much the desk actually trusts FX direction right now.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: December is the dollar's worst month: down vs the G10 average in 75% of years since 2010
items.idea: Using base-neutral G10 returns for 2010-2025, the dollar averages -0.65% in December and is negative about 75% of the time; over the last decade the average is about -1.06%. The franc averages +0.64% and beat the G10 average in 81% of Decembers (89% recently); the krona averages +0.84% with a 69% hit rate, both with t-stats near 2.4. Long SEK/USD has averaged +1.45% in December with a 75% hit rate. The one big failure was 2014, when Riksbank easing met a Fed turning hawkish.
items.angle: This year looks more like the 2014 exception (hawkish Fed) than the average. CHF is the seasonal play that survives a hawkish Fed; SEK is not.
items.tweetA: Dollar seasonality in December: negative 3 years out of 4, average -1.06% over the last decade. The one year it failed badly was 2014, when the Fed was turning hawkish. Guess what the Fed is priced to do this December.
items.tweetB: Two currencies have a real December edge: SEK and CHF, both with t-stats around 2.4. One is a high-beta cyclical, the other is a haven. In a year with the S&P down 12%, only one of those seasonals is worth trusting.

charts.desc: G10 monthly seasonality heatmap (base-neutral returns, 2010-2025) plus year-by-year December returns for long SEK/USD.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: The Australian dollar has stopped trading US yields. It now trades copper and the AI capex cycle
items.idea: On 30-day rolling correlations, AUD/USD shows almost no link to US yields but 0.49 with the S&P 500, 0.54 with MSCI World and 0.52 with copper. USD/JPY still tracks Treasury yields (0.66 to the 2-year, 0.62 to the 10-year). USD/ZAR runs at about -0.81 to gold, USD/KRW moves inversely to global equities, and USD/CLP follows copper. MUFG ties copper's correction to investors cutting AI-related industrial exposure, given data-centre power and transmission demand.
items.angle: AUD, CLP and KRW have become liquid proxies for AI infrastructure sentiment. Useful as hedges for an AI book that cannot short the equities.
items.tweetA: AUD/USD correlation with copper: 0.52. With US yields: roughly zero. The Aussie dollar is now an AI capex derivative, because data centers need copper. If you're long the buildout and want a cheap hedge, it's sitting in FX.
items.tweetB: USD/ZAR vs gold: -0.81 correlation. Gold is down 29% this year. The rand is the levered expression of the precious-metals unwind and almost nobody outside EM desks is watching it.

charts.desc: 30-day rolling correlation matrix across G10 and EM FX, equities, yields, oil, gold and copper.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / MUFG FX Weekly
items.title: US payrolls went from 10k a month in 2025 to a 137k three-month average, with wages drifting to 3%
items.idea: Ahead of the Dec 4 jobs report MUFG notes payroll growth averaged about 137,000 a month in the three months to October and 86,000 over ten months, against roughly 10,000 a month in 2025. Unemployment is just above 4% and higher participation has held average hourly earnings growth near 3%. MUFG expects the data to back another 25bp hike in December; euro-area CPI on Dec 1 is expected at about twice the ECB's target.
items.angle: Jobs accelerating while wage growth slows is a supply story. That argues the inflation problem is energy, not labor, which is the case for a short hiking cycle.
items.tweetA: Payrolls: 10k/month in 2025, 137k/month now. Wage growth: falling toward 3%. The labor market is getting stronger and cheaper at the same time. The Fed is hiking into an energy shock, not a wage spiral, and those end differently.
items.tweetB: The Fed is priced to hike in December with unemployment near 4%, payrolls re-accelerating and the S&P down 12%. Dec 4 payrolls is the last data point that can change that. Consensus is a hike at 93%. I'd watch participation, not the headline.

charts.desc: Charts inside, worth opening.

items.title: Citadel Securities calls it late 2018: S&P -12.3%, PCE 3.8%, GDP 4.3%, 93% odds of a December hike
items.idea: The S&P 500 is down 12.3% from its October high. On Wednesday PCE printed 3.8% (a five-month high) and Q3 GDP 4.3% against 3.5% expected, and prediction markets moved to 93% for a 25bp December hike. A Bloomberg overlay rebased to Dec 31 shows 2026 tracking 2018 closely. Citadel's four shared pillars: a strong dollar (+9.3% in nine months then, +7.0% now), weak cyclicals, high yields (3.25% peak then, 5.34% this year) and earnings estimates rolling over. In 2018, about 11% of the 19.8% drop came between Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve.
items.angle: The analog's last act is the Powell pivot. With inflation at 3.8% instead of 2%, the pivot is the part that may not repeat.
items.tweetA: The 2018 analog works until the last scene. In 2018 the Fed pivoted with core inflation at 2%. Today PCE is 3.8% and GDP just printed 4.3%. Same chart, no rescue. That's the part of the overlay nobody is pricing.
items.tweetB: In 2018 the 10-year peaked at 3.25% and the market broke. This year it peaked at 5.34% and the S&P is down 12%. Either equities have become far more rate-tolerant, or the adjustment isn't finished. I don't think it's the first one.

charts.desc: S&P 500 in 2026 vs 2018, both rebased to 100 at Dec 31, with the Thanksgiving-to-Christmas window boxed.

items.title: The 2018 playbook in numbers: hike into a -15% market, lose another 7% in three sessions, pivot two weeks later
items.idea: From Sep 20 to Dec 24, 2018 the S&P fell 19.8% (2,930 to 2,351), the Nasdaq 23.6% and the Russell 2000 27.2%. High-yield spreads widened from about 316 to 530bp and the VIX closed at 36.1, while the 10-year fell from 3.24% to 2.74% and gold gained about 7%. The Fed hiked on Dec 19 with the market already down 15%; stocks lost another 7% in three sessions. Powell said 'patience' on Jan 4 and the index was back at highs by late April. Q3 2018 GDP was 3.4% and cuts were priced two quarters later.
items.angle: Bonds and gold hedged in 2018 because growth fear beat inflation fear. With PCE at 3.8% that hand-off has not happened yet; watch for the 10-year to start falling on bad equity days.
items.tweetA: In Q4 2018 the 10-year fell 50bp and gold rose 7% while stocks dropped 20%. This year gold is -29% and the 10-year peaked at 5.34%. The hedges that worked in the analog are the things that have been getting sold. That's the real difference.
items.tweetB: HY spreads went from 316 to 530bp in the 2018 episode. If you want to know whether this is 2018 or something worse, stop looking at the S&P overlay and look at credit. Equities reprice multiples. Credit reprices earnings.

charts.desc: Charts of the 2018 cross-asset moves. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.title: Dollar +10%, gold -29%, silver -60%: silver is falling 2.1x as fast as gold, the most of any episode
items.idea: Year to date the dollar ETF is up 10.11%, gold is down 28.94% and silver 60.34%. Silver spiked about 13% in early January in a blow-off and then lost nearly two-thirds of its value. In 2011-2015 the dollar gained about 35% while gold fell 45% and silver 72%; in 2022 a 19% dollar rally came with gold -22% and silver -35%. Silver normally falls 1.4-1.6x as much as gold. This year the ratio is 2.1.
items.angle: A 2.1x beta says this is deleveraging of a crowded retail and momentum position, not just a dollar move. Capitulation ratios like this tend to mark late stages.
items.tweetA: Silver is down 60% from a January blow-off, falling 2.1x as fast as gold. In 2011-15 and 2022 the ratio was 1.4 to 1.6. When the beta itself breaks its range, you're not watching a macro repricing, you're watching forced sellers. $SLV
items.tweetB: Ten months ago the consensus was 'the dollar is finished, metals to the moon.' Dollar +10%, gold -29%, silver -60%. The lesson isn't about gold. It's that the trade everyone describes as an article of faith is the one with no buyers left.

charts.desc: YTD performance of the dollar ETF vs gold and silver, with the January silver blow-off visible.

items.title: Once the S&P is down 10%, history says 80% odds it reaches -15% and just under 60% it reaches -20%
items.idea: Since 2007 the S&P has been in a drawdown of 10% or more about 50% of the time and 20% or more about 29% of the time. Simple conditional math on those base rates gives about 80% odds of -15% and a little under 60% of -20% once -10% is crossed. Recoveries: 5 months and +28% in 12 months after 2015-16; 4 months and +37% after Q4 2018; 5 months and +75% after Covid; 15 months after 2022, when rates and earnings fell together.
items.angle: The author's own caveat is that this is a blunt instrument: it uses time spent in drawdown, not the count of episodes. Useful for sizing, not for timing.
items.tweetA: At -12.3% the base rate says roughly 4-in-5 odds of -15% and better than a coin flip on -20%. Double-digit corrections rarely stop at -10. If your plan is 'buy the dip', the dip you're planning for is probably not this one.
items.tweetB: Recovery times after big drawdowns: 4 months, 5 months, 5 months, and 15 months. The outlier is 2022, the only one where rates and earnings fell together. Multiple compression heals fast. Earnings compression doesn't. That's the whole question for 2027.

charts.desc: S&P 500 drawdown chart since 2007 with frequency table for -10% and -20% drawdowns.

items.title: Sky's cofounder borrowed 77M USDS against his own token, and now depositors can withdraw $78k of $158.6M
items.idea: Rune Christensen said he still owes about 77 million USDS on loans backed by his staked SKY, and that the debt is part of why stUSDS depositors cannot exit. Bitquery traced about $77.1M of pool debt to a wallet linked to rune.eth and about $40M to the Sky Frontier Foundation. On Friday Spark's data showed $78,231 available against about $158.6M deposited. Sky is fast-tracking a vote to send the foundation 25M USDS to pay down its debt, and Upbit has halted SKY and USDS deposits.
items.angle: About three-quarters of the pool was lent to the founder and his foundation against the governance token. This is related-party lending in a DeFi wrapper, and it sits behind one of the largest decentralized stablecoins.
items.tweetA: A lending pool where the two biggest borrowers are the founder and the founder's foundation, borrowing against the protocol's own token. $117M of a $158M pool. DeFi spent five years rebuilding the exact bank it said it was replacing.
items.tweetB: $78,231 available to withdraw against $158.6M in deposits. That's 0.05% liquidity. The fix being voted on is the protocol sending 25M to its own foundation to repay the protocol. Read that twice.

items.title: Trump's third meme coin dinner drew $8.6M in holdings, down from $148M
items.idea: Top $TRUMP holders brought a combined $8.6M in tokens to the third dinner at Trump's Virginia golf club, against $148M at the May 2025 dinner per Reuters. Justin Sun, top holder last time with $18.5M, skipped it. The token hit a record low near $0.79, about 99% below its January 2025 peak of $73.43. Rep. Maxine Waters, in line to chair House Financial Services, says the first crypto bill will be her Stop TRUMP in Crypto Act; she cites disclosures showing at least $635M to the family.
items.angle: With Democrats taking both chambers in January, the regulatory tailwind for crypto flips to oversight and investigations. That is a 2027 headline risk for the whole sector.
items.tweetA: $TRUMP is down 99% and the family made $635M. Dinner attendance by wallet size fell 94%. The token did exactly what it was designed to do. The only people surprised are the ones holding it.
items.tweetB: The incoming House Financial Services chair says her first crypto bill targets the president's own token. For two years the industry priced regulation as a tailwind. In January that flips, and I don't think alts have noticed.

items.title: Bitcoin hit $55,100, a two-year low, and could not hold a bounce on Nvidia's 31% day
items.idea: Bitcoin fell to about $55,100 early last Saturday, its lowest since September 2024, as an AI-stock rout took about 10% off Nasdaq 100 futures in a week. Nvidia then reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and closed up 31%; bitcoin briefly topped $64,000 before sliding back near $60,000, below its pre-news level. It traded around $60,100 Friday, about a third below the roughly $90,500 of last Thanksgiving.
items.angle: BTC took the full downside of the AI liquidation and none of the relief rally. That asymmetry is what a market with no marginal buyer looks like.
items.tweetA: Nvidia closed +31% in a day and bitcoin ended lower than before the news. $BTC got all of the AI drawdown and none of the bounce. When an asset only keeps the downside correlation, the bid is gone.
items.tweetB: Bitcoin is $60k, a third below last Thanksgiving, with a hawkish Fed, a strong dollar and gold down 29%. It's trading like what it is in this regime: a long-duration liquidity asset. The 'digital gold' pitch at least got the correlation right.

items.title: Binance reopens 28 days after a $6.3B hack; 44% of the loot is frozen, vs 3% after Bybit
items.idea: Binance said its withdrawal suspension is fully lifted 28 days after hackers drained hot wallets of about $6.3B. It covered losses from its futures insurance fund, treasury and SAFU, putting up more than $6.34B. Elliptic says about $2.85B (44%) has been frozen or seized. The DOJ filed a civil forfeiture case for more than $1.1B in USDC it says Lazarus Group stole; if forfeited, Circle will mint replacement USDC for the government.
items.angle: The freeze rate going from 3% to 44% in a year is the real story: stablecoin issuers are now an enforcement arm. That cuts both ways for the 'censorship-resistant' pitch.
items.tweetA: After Bybit, 3% of the stolen funds were frozen. After Binance, 44%. The difference is issuers who can freeze and re-mint on a court order. Stablecoins are becoming the most enforceable money ever built, and that's the product.
items.tweetB: Binance absorbed a $6.3B loss from its own balance sheet and reopened in 28 days. No bailout, no bankruptcy, no haircut for users. Whatever you think of the exchange, it turned out to hold the capital. That's a stress test most of crypto never passed.

items.title: Bitcoin printed C$24,250 on Kraken's Canadian book, a 71% gap, and the trades stand
items.idea: Overnight into last Saturday bitcoin fell from about C$84,150 to C$24,250 on Kraken's CAD market while the USD market never went below $55,100. Kraken's own USD/CAD pair printed as low as 0.30 against about 1.43. About 616 BTC traded on the pair overnight, much of it in the first 15 minutes of each hour. Kraken says the platform processed every order correctly, found no breach, and executed trades stand. Adam Back attributes it to a lack of CAD bids.
items.angle: Thin fiat pairs have no market makers when vol spikes on a weekend. Stop orders on secondary books are a free option for whoever is resting bids.
items.tweetA: Bitcoin traded at a 71% discount on a regulated exchange for hours and nobody arbitraged it. That tells you how much balance sheet is actually deployed in crypto market-making on a weekend: none. The trades stand.
items.tweetB: 616 BTC traded on Kraken's CAD book, clustered in the first 15 minutes of each hour. That's not panic, that's a TWAP algo selling into an empty book all night. Somebody's execution bot donated a fortune to the only bidder awake.

items.title: An intruder reached client data at Zodia Custody while Standard Chartered's buyout awaits approval
items.idea: Zodia Custody, which Standard Chartered agreed last month to buy outright, said an unauthorized party reached a limited set of client data. It spotted probing on Nov 23, switched off its business API, and found the access the next day. Exposed data were public organization details and, for a small number of clients and employees, a business contact name and email. No unauthorized transactions have been found; it has not said how many clients were hit or how the intruder got in.
items.angle: Small breach, bad timing. Bank-owned custody sells on security, and this lands in the same month as the Binance hack and with a regulatory approval pending.
items.tweetA: Bank-grade custody's whole pitch is 'we are not an exchange.' A month after a $6.3B exchange hack, a bank-owned custodian finds an intruder through its API. Contact data only, this time. The attack surface is the integration layer, not the vault.
items.tweetB: Standard Chartered agreed to buy Zodia outright last month. This month, a breach disclosure while the deal awaits regulators. Every bank acquiring crypto infrastructure just got a preview of what their first incident report looks like.

items.title: Ansem says his wallet was drained through his own trading app. On-chain analysts doubt it
items.idea: Trader Ansem said a Solana wallet was drained via his profile on Bullpen, an app he co-founded, where he had imported the private key. The wallet sold ANSEM, which fell 60% within an hour; about 2.15M USDC went to an Arbitrum wallet. Researcher MLM says the activity 'looks nothing like a hack', pointing to a dormant wallet he tagged as Ansem's a year ago that funded the proceeds wallet about an hour before the selling.
items.angle: Influencer tokens have no disclosure regime, so 'hack' is unfalsifiable. One more data point for why personality coins stay uninvestable.
items.tweetA: A token named after an influencer drops 60% in an hour after his wallet sells it. He says hack. The chain says a wallet linked to him funded the destination an hour earlier. There's no version of this story where holders were protected.
items.tweetB: He imported a private key into an app he co-founded and it got drained. If that's true, the product is unsafe. If it isn't, the founder is. Either way the app has a problem.

items.title: OKX and NYSE-owner ICE launch tokenized stocks in the US. 67 companies including Apple and Nvidia object
items.idea: OKXICE opened Monday to eligible US OKX customers with six stocks (Coinbase, Securitize, Strategy, BitGo, Robinhood, Circle) paired with USDC, each token backed by one real share; another 113 stocks, ETFs and ETPs are staged. 67 companies including Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla have objected to their shares trading there. It runs under the SEC's September Innovation Exemption, which Senate Banking Democrats led by Van Hollen and Warren want withdrawn. Warren also wants proposed Regulation Crypto Assets (raises up to $75M a year) scrapped.
items.angle: The owner of the NYSE is building the venue that competes with the NYSE, under an exemption the incoming Senate majority wants revoked.
items.tweetA: The owner of the New York Stock Exchange now runs a venue where you buy Coinbase stock with USDC. Its co-chair is Andrew Cuomo. 67 issuers have objected. If you wanted proof tokenization is a market-structure fight and not a tech upgrade, here it is. $ICE
items.tweetB: Tokenized equities in the US exist because of one SEC exemption from September. Democrats take the Senate in January and have already asked for it to be pulled. A venue built on an exemption has oversight risk from day one. Builders should price that.

items.title: Ethereum makes quantum and AI cryptanalysis its top priority, calls it harder than the Merge 'and we have less time'
items.idea: The Ethereum Foundation said defending against quantum computers and AI-assisted cryptanalysis is now its top priority and has doubled its protocol security team. It backs hash-based cryptography to replace elliptic curves across blobs, wallets and validator keys, recommends Keccak-256 as the single hash, and keeps an internal 2029 deadline pending a January review. Separately the Zakura team asked Zcash to close its older Sapling pool (about 400,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of supply) to new funds, citing a machine-checked proof of the Riemann hypothesis by an Anthropic mathematician and an unconfirmed rumor that AI labs can factor large numbers much faster.
items.angle: The threat model has changed from 'quantum hardware someday' to 'AI finds a better algorithm any day'. That is undatable, which is why they are moving now. Bitcoin has the same curve and no migration plan this organized.
items.tweetA: Ethereum just ranked 'AI breaks our cryptography' above every scaling upgrade. The old threat was a quantum computer you could see coming. The new one is a math result that arrives on a random Tuesday. $ETH has a 2029 plan. What's Bitcoin's?
items.tweetB: A Zcash team wants to close a shielded pool because of a rumor that AI labs can factor faster. They admit it's speculative. That's the point: when the downside is every key at once, you act on rumors. Watch who else starts migrating quietly.

items.title: Ethereum devs keep the contested gas repricing; Hoodi testnet fork set for Dec 15
items.idea: Core developers agreed to keep Glamsterdam's EIP-8037 as written and fork the Hoodi testnet on Dec 15. The change raises the cost of creating new accounts, storage and contract code, and app developers had pushed to stop it. No client team vetoed; Erigon's Andrew Ashikhmin called it possibly 'the lesser evil'. Forking the testnet on the unchanged spec effectively commits mainnet, with no date set.
items.angle: State growth is being priced for the first time. That raises costs for apps that mint many accounts or contracts and favours L2s and stateless designs.
items.tweetA: Ethereum is about to charge more for creating state: new accounts, storage, contracts. App developers fought it and lost. This is the base layer telling apps to go live on L2s, written into the fee schedule. $ETH
items.tweetB: 'Nobody's particularly happy, but we need to take a pragmatic view.' That's how a core protocol change got approved. Ethereum governance now sounds exactly like a standards committee, which is what a settlement layer should sound like.

items.title: The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill reaches the House calendar with weeks left before Democrats take over
items.idea: H.R. 8957 reached the House calendar after the Financial Services Committee filed its report, making it eligible for a floor vote with no date set. It would bar Treasury from selling, swapping or pledging reserve bitcoin for 20 years, then cap sales at 10% of the reserve every two years. It cleared committee 28-21 in September; Rep. Jared Golden is the only Democrat among 23 cosponsors. It still needs the House, Senate and president before Democrats take both chambers in January.
items.angle: A 20-year no-sale lock would remove government-held coins from float permanently. The odds of passing the Senate in a lame duck look low, and the market is not pricing it at all with BTC at $60k.
items.tweetA: The bitcoin reserve bill would lock the government's coins for 20 years, then allow selling 10% every two years. It has one Democratic cosponsor and about five weeks. $BTC at $60k tells you what the market thinks the odds are.
items.tweetB: Lame-duck Congress has two things on the clock: a bitcoin reserve bill with one Democratic cosponsor and a permitting bill that passed the Senate 62-33. Only one of those is bipartisan. Position accordingly.

items.title: Kalshi dodges an emergency shutdown in New York and leaves Utah to end a 14-count criminal case
items.idea: A New York judge signaled she will deny the attorney general's request for an emergency order against Kalshi, noting the status quo 'has been going on for over a year', and offered January dates for a preliminary injunction plus limits for 18-to-20-year-olds. Kalshi argued that because it is New York-based the order would shut it down for every customer everywhere. Utah's AG asked to drop a 14-count criminal case, without prejudice, after Kalshi stopped new trades for more than 177,000 Utah users.
items.angle: State criminal charges are the new lever against prediction markets, and Kalshi blinked in Utah. Federal preemption is not holding as cleanly as the bull case assumed.
items.tweetA: Kalshi walked away from 177,000 users in Utah to make criminal charges disappear. That's the price of a state fight, and there are 49 more states. Prediction markets' federal-preemption thesis is getting tested one attorney general at a time.
items.tweetB: The macro letters in my inbox today quote prediction-market odds for the Fed (93% hike) as the reference price. The same week, one state charges the venue criminally and another tries to shut it down. The product won before the law caught up.

items.title: FTX's former COO says Netflix's 'The Altruists' gets the collapse wrong
items.idea: Constance Wang, former FTX COO, told Laura Shin the Netflix miniseries is built around a Bankman-Fried/Ellison romance she did not know about until after the bankruptcy, and that it turns Ellison into a mastermind, crediting her with the seven versions of Alameda's balance sheet sent to Genesis. She calls the portrayal of CZ racist. She says her last conversation with Bankman-Fried before extradition convinced her the human cost never entered his expected-value math.
items.angle: FTX is now prestige TV while Bitcoin is at a two-year low and Binance was just hacked for $6.3B. The cultural memory of crypto is being written as a fraud story at the worst point in the cycle.
items.tweetA: Netflix made the FTX collapse a love story. The detail that matters is the one the insider flags: seven versions of one balance sheet sent to a lender. The fraud was a spreadsheet problem. TV can't film a spreadsheet, so it filmed a romance.
items.tweetB: Bitcoin at a 2-year low, a $6.3B exchange hack, and a Netflix series about FTX, all in one month. Retail's next impression of crypto is being shaped right now, and it isn't by anyone in the industry.

items.title: Goldman initiates Unitree at Sell with 48% downside. The stock goes limit-up the next day
items.idea: On Thursday Goldman's Jacqueline Du initiated Unitree (688836.SS) at Sell with a Rmb347.10 target against a Rmb666 close, implying almost 48% downside. On Friday the stock rose about 19.9% to Rmb798.70, taking market cap toward Rmb323bn, roughly $48bn. The author notes Street targets for the same robotics opportunity are landing wildly far apart.
items.angle: At Rmb798.70 the Goldman target is now 57% below the price. When the first bulge-bracket valuation is ignored within 24 hours, the stock is trading on policy and flows, not on a model.
items.tweetA: Goldman put a Sell on Unitree with a target 48% lower. Next day: limit-up. The target is now 57% below the price. A $48B humanoid robot company is trading on policy flow, and a DCF is not a tool for that market.
items.tweetB: Unitree at $48B is worth more than most global auto suppliers, for a company whose product is still mostly in demos. I don't know what it's worth either. But when analysts can't agree within a factor of two, the option value is the stock.

items.title: China's STAR 50 jumped 15% in one session after Beijing encouraged more stock-market support
items.idea: The catalyst for Unitree's limit-up was Beijing's decision to encourage additional stock-market support, with the STAR 50 surging 15% on Friday in a broader recovery. This comes in the same month as a global AI-stock liquidation that took the S&P 500 down 12.3% from its high.
items.angle: Beijing is backstopping its tech equities while the Fed is hiking into a US drawdown. That is a policy divergence trade: China tech has a put, US tech does not.
items.tweetA: STAR 50 +15% in a day on state support. The same week the Fed is 93% priced to hike into a 12% S&P drawdown. One AI market has a policy put and the other has a central bank selling it. That gap is tradeable. $KWEB
items.tweetB: Beijing answered the AI liquidation by telling the market to buy. Washington's answer is a rate hike priced at 93% for December. Whatever you think of the method, capital notices which government wants its tech stocks higher.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Unitree
items.title: Humanoid robots: hardware costs are falling fast, and that is the problem for margins
items.idea: The piece's framing of the Goldman view: hardware economics are improving rapidly, but falling selling prices combined with increasingly accessible AI software raise questions about future profitability. The move from lab demos to commercially productive machines could completely rearrange today's competitive ranking.
items.angle: This is the solar-panel and EV pattern: volume leaders in a deflating hardware category rarely keep the profit pool. Value may sit in components, actuators and deployment instead of the humanoid brand.
items.tweetA: Humanoid robots are following the solar script: costs collapse, volumes explode, and the manufacturers compete the margin to zero. The market is paying $48B for the company that makes the panel. I'd look at who sells the actuators.
items.tweetB: If the robot brain becomes a commodity model anyone can license, and the body gets cheaper every quarter, what exactly is the moat? Today's leaderboard is a demo leaderboard. The winners get decided on the factory floor, and that's a different skill.

items.title: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 loops the same layers twice and claims 2-3 trillion-parameter performance from a 750B model
items.idea: GLM-5.4 is Z.ai's first flagship on a loop transformer: it runs 28 layers of the 750B GLM-5 base twice per token, adapted through continued training instead of training from scratch. The second pass reuses the first pass's sparse KV cache and attention indices, so it costs one sliding window of cache, not a full context. In a 30B ablation with about 10% more training compute, looping lifted AIME25 from 19.17 to 30.42 and GPQA-Diamond from 47.58 to 56.26, with outputs 10-14% shorter. It runs at up to 200 tokens/s off-peak; weights are planned after safety hardening.
items.angle: Depth through recurrence trades parameters (memory) for compute (FLOPs per token). For a lab short of high-end memory and GPUs, that is a way around hardware limits, and it shifts inference demand toward compute over memory at the margin.
items.tweetA: A Chinese lab just got a 59% jump on a math benchmark for ~10% more training compute by running the same layers twice. If depth can be rented at inference instead of bought in parameters, the 'bigger model needs more HBM' math gets less linear. $MU
items.tweetB: Export controls limit how big a model China can train. So Z.ai stopped making the model bigger and made it think twice. Constraint breeds architecture. This is the second-order effect of chip bans nobody models.

items.title: Multi-agent debate does not beat the same compute spent on independent votes
items.idea: A paper on 'Recursive Collective Intelligence' grades agent teams against as many independent agents as the same token budget buys. Debate, shared blackboards and delegating coordinators stayed at or below the compute-matched vote on six shared-information benchmarks. Teams win only when information is split: on HiddenBench four 27B agents with split facts scored 0.959 vs 0.942 for one agent holding everything. Identical agents formed a hub in about a third of runs, adding 18 points, and self-organizing groups spent about two-thirds of tokens on coordination. Label-free self-training kept improving for four to six generations.
items.angle: This is the Coase theorem for agents: organization pays only where information is distributed. Most 'agent swarm' products run on shared context and are paying a two-thirds coordination tax for nothing.
items.tweetA: Agent teams spend two-thirds of their tokens coordinating and still lose to a simple majority vote, unless each agent knows something the others don't. That's not an AI finding. That's every corporate meeting, measured for the first time.
items.tweetB: Most multi-agent startups sell 'a team of AIs debating'. The data: debate ties or loses to a vote at equal compute. The only setup that wins is when information is split across agents. The value is in private data access, not in the org chart.

items.title: One week of agent news: 948 kernel exploits from an OpenAI pipeline, a sandbox-escape test, and agents rewriting an API in Rust
items.idea: Headline list from the issue (details truncated in the email): an OpenAI pipeline finds 948 kernel exploits; Anthropic tests sandbox escape with 'Siren' and launches 'Claude Ship'; Claude agents migrate the Messages API to Rust; OpenAI and Cisco open-source 'Shirudo'; Cognition ships SWE-2.1; Ramp Labs introduces speculative encoding; ShellBench tests agents on everyday work.
items.angle: Automated exploit discovery at that scale changes the economics of both offense and patching. It links directly to Ethereum reprioritising around AI-assisted cryptanalysis this week.
items.tweetA: 948 kernel exploits from one automated pipeline. That is more than any human team can triage, let alone fix. The patch queue is now the bottleneck in security, not the discovery, and every unpatched fleet is on a clock. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: Same week: an AI pipeline finds 948 kernel exploits and Ethereum declares AI cryptanalysis its top priority. Two unrelated teams reaching the same conclusion about attack costs. Security budgets haven't repriced for this yet.

items.title: The House votes this week on BAAJA, a permitting bill that already passed the Senate 62-33
items.idea: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, led by Senators Heinrich, Whitehouse, Capito and Lee, would curtail litigation risk under NEPA and NHPA while keeping substantive environmental protections, and give the federal government backstop authority to site and permit transmission lines. Smith calls it the most important permitting legislation in our lifetimes. Unions back it; the Sierra Club and NRDC oppose it. Some House Democrats want to wait for the next Congress after winning both chambers.
items.angle: Federal backstop siting for transmission is the single biggest unlock for grid capex. A House pass this week would be a direct catalyst for transmission builders and equipment names.
items.tweetA: A permitting bill with federal transmission siting authority passed the Senate 62-33 and hits the House this week. If it passes, the binding constraint on US power moves from lawyers to transformers. $PWR $ETN $GEV are the read-through.
items.tweetB: The AI trade just got liquidated and the best thing that could happen to its power bottleneck is sitting on the House floor. Nobody on my feed is talking about BAAJA. The market trades GPUs and forgets you need a permit to plug them in.

charts.desc: Chart showing how hard it has become to build in the US. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.title: 64% of solar projects needing a full environmental review got sued, and 32% were cancelled
items.idea: Of solar projects that required an environmental impact statement between 2010 and 2018, 64% were sued and 32% were ultimately cancelled, both higher rates than for fossil fuel projects. Stapp's argument is that the procedural rules in NEPA and NHPA create a 'litigation doom loop': a judge can enjoin a project if an agency missed any impact a plaintiff can think of, which raises costs and shrinks the set of projects developers even attempt.
items.angle: Environmental procedure law now blocks clean energy more than fossil. That reframes permitting reform as the climate position, and explains why Senate climate hawks are leading the bill.
items.tweetA: One in three large solar projects that went through full environmental review got cancelled. Two in three got sued. The law written to protect the environment is the main thing stopping clean power. Fossil projects had better odds.
items.tweetB: A 32% cancellation rate is a cost of capital, not a statistic. Price a one-in-three chance of zero into any project and half the pipeline never gets proposed. The real cost of NEPA litigation is the projects nobody bothered to file.

charts.desc: Charts inside, worth opening.

items.title: The US is worse at permitting and building transmission lines today than it was ten years ago
items.idea: Stapp shows a chart indicating the US is getting fewer transmission lines permitted and built now than a decade ago, at a time of rising electricity demand. He argues transmission is the first-order need for electrification: moving power from where it is generated to where it is used.
items.angle: Demand is up and line-miles are down. That gap is why behind-the-meter gas and on-site generation became the default for data centers, and why interconnection queues keep growing.
items.tweetA: Electricity demand is rising for the first time in a generation and the US builds fewer transmission lines than it did 10 years ago. That gap doesn't close with more solar panels. It closes with on-site gas turbines, which is exactly what data centers are buying. $GEV
items.tweetB: Everyone models AI power demand. Almost nobody models the wire. Generation without transmission is stranded, and the US has been cutting its build rate for a decade. The scarce asset in this cycle is the right-of-way.

charts.desc: US transmission line-miles built per year, declining over the last decade.

items.title: Why 'wait for a better deal' fails: no veto-proof majority, and the incoming chairs opposed every past bill
items.idea: Stapp's case against waiting: Democrats won both chambers but lack veto-proof majorities, so any deal still needs Trump's signature and, with the filibuster, at least four Senate Republicans. The likely incoming chairs, Rep. Jared Huffman (House Natural Resources) and Sen. Jeff Merkley (Senate EPW), opposed all three prior deals: BAES in 2022 (failed 47-47, Senate Democrats 40-10 in favour), the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act (passed House Democrats 165-46, Senate 46-5) and EPRA in 2024. Merkley twice objected to a bipartisan manager's amendment on BAAJA, the second time after the bill had already passed.
items.angle: Committee chairs set the agenda, so the January handover is a real deadline. If BAAJA dies this week, assume no federal permitting reform before 2029.
items.tweetA: The lame duck is the last window for permitting reform until 2029. The two people about to chair the relevant committees voted against every deal for five years, including the ones most of their own party backed. This week's House vote is the whole ballgame.
items.tweetB: In 2022 the League of Conservation Voters scored a vote against transmission reform as the pro-environment vote, rewarding Republicans who killed a Democratic bill. That's how an interest group ends up opposing its own stated goal. Watch incentives, not mission statements.

items.title: The permitting fight has split the Democratic coalition: unions for, big green groups against
items.idea: Union workers have come out strongly for BAAJA while the Sierra Club and NRDC oppose it. Smith's framing: the anti-development regime looked fine in the 1990s and 2000s when software and finance drove growth and manufacturing was outsourced to China, but it only pushed physical challenges into the future. Stapp calls the result a 'tyranny of the minority', where a small unrepresentative group holds a veto over anything anyone dislikes.
items.angle: The coalition is realigning around building versus blocking. Labor siding with permitting reform is the durable political base for the reindustrialisation trade, whichever party holds Congress.
items.tweetA: Unions and environmental groups are on opposite sides of the biggest infrastructure bill of the decade. The fight over building things is now inside the Democratic party, and the hard hats are winning Senate votes 62-33.
items.tweetB: For 30 years America could afford not to build because growth came from software and finance. Now growth needs power lines, fabs and data centers. The rules were written for an economy that no longer exists. That's the reindustrialisation thesis in one sentence.
